passages.title: The repair economy and the value of keeping things
passages.text:
A product is often treated as obsolete when a newer version appears, even though the older object may still perform its original function. The habit of replacement is supported by commercial incentives, but it is also shaped by design choices. Devices may be assembled with glued components, proprietary fasteners or software restrictions that make ordinary repairs difficult. A cracked screen or a worn battery can then turn a largely functional object into waste. The cost of repair is not simply the price of a part; it includes the time, information and tools needed to reach the damaged component.

Repair advocates argue that extending the useful life of goods can reduce demand for raw materials and lower the volume of discarded products. The environmental gain, however, is not automatic. A repair that consumes unusual parts shipped across long distances may have a different footprint from one using locally available components. An old appliance that uses substantially more electricity than a modern efficient model may also be worth replacing. Good policy therefore needs to compare the full life-cycle consequences rather than assume that repair is always preferable.

Access to information is central. Manufacturers may publish manuals and spare-part catalogues, while independent technicians may rely on community forums, diagnostic tools and experience. When repair information is withheld or software disables a replacement component, consumers can become dependent on a single authorised network. On the other hand, poorly designed repairs can create safety risks, especially where batteries, electrical insulation or pressure systems are involved. The case for repairability is strongest when products are designed to be opened safely and when reliable parts and instructions are available.

A repair economy also has a social dimension. Local repair shops can create skilled work, preserve practical knowledge and make essential equipment affordable to households that cannot replace it easily. Yet these benefits require training and a dependable supply of components. A city cannot build a repair ecosystem merely by encouraging people to keep broken objects in cupboards. Collection systems, vocational education and fair access to diagnostic information matter.

The useful question is not whether society should reject new technology. It is whether innovation must always make yesterday’s product difficult to maintain. A durable product can still be upgraded, and a repairable product can still be replaced when its performance or safety justifies doing so. The aim is to make repair a genuine option rather than a costly exception, allowing consumers to compare durability, energy use, price and environmental consequences before deciding what to do.

passages.title: When a city measures what it cannot see
passages.text:
Urban governments increasingly use dashboards to describe how a city is functioning. A dashboard may display average travel time, air quality, water consumption, school attendance or the number of complaints resolved. Such measures can help officials identify patterns that would otherwise remain hidden. They can also make a complex service easier for residents to question: a target that is publicly stated can be compared with the result that follows.

But a metric is not the same as the thing it represents. A transport department that counts buses may report growth even when routes do not connect workers to the places they need to reach. A water authority may report fewer interruptions while some low-income neighbourhoods continue to receive unreliable supply. A school system may improve attendance statistics by changing how absences are recorded without improving the quality of teaching. Once a measure becomes a target, organisations may concentrate on improving the number rather than the underlying service.

This does not make measurement useless. It makes the design of measurement a matter of judgement. A useful indicator should be connected to a public purpose, understandable to people outside the department and capable of being checked independently. It should also reveal distribution. A citywide average can improve while a particular ward becomes worse off. Breaking results down by neighbourhood, income group or time of day may expose a problem that an overall figure conceals. At the same time, excessive subdivision can create unstable numbers or reveal personal information, so transparency must be balanced with privacy and statistical reliability.

Residents can contribute knowledge that administrative data do not contain. A complaint log may show where people report broken streetlights, but it will not necessarily show where residents have stopped reporting because they expect no response. A map of public toilets may record their location without revealing whether they are clean, accessible or open at the hours when workers need them. Field observation, surveys and community meetings can help explain why a numerical pattern exists.

The strongest civic dashboard therefore combines indicators with explanation. It records what is being measured, how the measure is calculated, who is missing from the data and what action will follow. It does not pretend that every valuable outcome can be reduced to a single score. Measurement is most useful when it helps public institutions learn, invites scrutiny and keeps attention on the experience of residents rather than the appearance of administrative success.

passages.title: The case for slow reading
passages.text:
The modern reader encounters more text in a day than many earlier generations encountered in a week, yet quantity does not necessarily produce understanding. Messages, headlines, notifications and short summaries arrive in fragments. A reader may recognise a topic repeatedly without ever following an argument from its premises to its conclusion. This creates a peculiar familiarity: the subject seems known because its vocabulary is familiar, while the relationships between its claims remain unexamined.

Slow reading is not simply reading at a low speed. It is a deliberate practice of returning to a sentence, asking what a pronoun refers to, distinguishing an example from a general rule and noticing when an author changes the meaning of a key term. It may involve pausing to compare two passages or checking whether a conclusion follows from the evidence offered. The practice is especially useful when a text is difficult, ambiguous or designed to persuade. A reader who moves quickly can still understand a simple account; a reader who moves slowly can still misunderstand a complicated one. The point is to give attention where the task requires it.

There is no need to romanticise printed pages or condemn digital media. A screen can support annotation, searching and comparison. A printed book can also be skimmed carelessly. The relevant difference lies in the habits encouraged by a particular environment. Frequent alerts make it harder to sustain attention, while a well-organised digital document may support close analysis. Teachers and editors can help by asking readers to explain not merely what a text says but how it reaches its conclusion.

Slow reading also has a democratic value. Public decisions are often presented through documents containing definitions, qualifications and exceptions. A citizen who reads only the headline may miss the condition that determines who is eligible, the date on which a rule begins or the evidence that has been left uncertain. Deliberate reading does not guarantee agreement, but it makes disagreement more informed. It allows people to identify the precise point at which their interpretations differ.

In a culture that rewards speed, careful reading may look inefficient. Its value becomes clear when the cost of a mistaken interpretation is high. The aim is not to read every message slowly. It is to recognise which texts deserve sustained attention and to approach them with enough patience to separate assertion, evidence and implication.

passages.title: Public spaces after the working day
passages.text:
A public square is often evaluated by how it looks during the day. Designers may assess its paving, planting, seating and visual connection to nearby buildings. Yet the square’s usefulness can change sharply after offices close, shops shut or public transport becomes less frequent. A space that feels welcoming at noon may become isolated in the evening if its edges are inactive, lighting is poor or people have no reason to remain there.

The evening economy is sometimes discussed only in terms of restaurants, entertainment and commercial activity. That view overlooks people who use public space without spending money. Shift workers may wait for a bus, students may meet after classes, and older residents may take a walk when the temperature falls. A square that depends entirely on businesses to remain lively can exclude those who cannot afford to buy something. Public seating, accessible toilets, drinking water and reliable transport are therefore not decorative additions; they help determine who can use the space and at what time.

Safety is also more complicated than installing brighter lights. Lighting can improve visibility, but it cannot by itself create a sense of welcome. A place may remain uncomfortable if there are long blank walls, hidden corners or no clear route to a busy street. Regular maintenance, visible public activity and the presence of people with different reasons to be there can matter as much as physical design. At the same time, crowding should not be treated as a universal solution: residents may need quiet, and events may disturb nearby homes.

Planning for different hours requires observation. Authorities can study pedestrian counts, speak with nearby residents and map the times when transport, public facilities and commercial services are available. They should distinguish between a temporary event that attracts a crowd and a routine pattern of everyday use. A festival can demonstrate that a square is capable of hosting people, but it does not prove that the space works on an ordinary Tuesday evening.

A successful public space is not necessarily busy every minute. It is one in which people can choose to be present without facing avoidable barriers. Designing for the evening means considering comfort, access, maintenance and the relationship between public and private activity. It also means accepting that the character of a place changes over time, and that good planning should accommodate that change rather than impose one fixed image of urban life.

passages.title: Fast Track Special Courts: continuity and capacity

sources.title: Cabinet approves continuation of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Fast Track Special Courts for a further period of five years
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Law and Justice

passages.text:
Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) are intended to support the expeditious trial of specified serious offences, including cases of rape and offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. Their purpose is not to create a separate standard of justice, but to improve the institutional capacity available to hear cases that can involve vulnerable complainants, complex evidence and substantial delays. A specialised court can focus judicial time and administrative support on a defined category of matters, although its effectiveness depends on staffing, prosecutors, infrastructure and the availability of witnesses.

On 4 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved continuation of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for FTSCs, including exclusive POCSO Courts, for a further five years: 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031. The government release stated a total outlay of ₹3,788.04 crore, comprising a Central share of ₹2,353.15 crore and a State/Union Territory share of ₹1,434.89 crore. It also stated that the Central share would be funded from the Nirbhaya Fund. The scheme provides for the operationalisation of 850 FTSCs, including exclusive POCSO Courts, across participating States and Union Territories.

The description of the scheme contains several distinct administrative ideas. A Centrally Sponsored Scheme involves financial participation by the Union and implementing responsibility shared with States or Union Territories. The Central and State/UT shares are not interchangeable labels; they identify the proposed division of the outlay. The number of courts represents planned operational capacity, not proof that every court is already functioning or that every case will be concluded within a particular period.

A court’s speed must also be assessed alongside fairness. Expedited proceedings should not mean that the accused loses a fair opportunity to respond, that witnesses are treated insensitively or that evidence is accepted without scrutiny. Delays can arise from vacancies, adjournments, forensic backlogs, service of process and the difficulty of securing attendance. A building or a court designation alone cannot resolve each of these constraints.

The policy question is therefore broader than whether a scheme has been extended. Monitoring should examine how many courts are operational, how cases move through the system, whether support services are available and whether judgments are delivered through fair procedures. The Cabinet decision establishes a funding and institutional framework for the next five-year period; evidence of outcomes must come from implementation and case-level performance, not from the approval announcement alone.

passages.title: VISTAR and the architecture of official statistics

sources.title: Cabinet approves Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research (VISTAR)
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

passages.text:
Official statistics are used to describe an economy and society: employment, prices, production, health, education and many other conditions. Their usefulness depends not only on the number of observations collected but also on whether the data arrive on time, can be compared across regions and are produced through transparent methods. When separate agencies use incompatible definitions or systems, even a large amount of data may be difficult to combine. The challenge is therefore institutional as well as technical.

On 4 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research, known as VISTAR. The Press Information Bureau release identified it as a central sector scheme for FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31, with an outlay of ₹4,371.10 crore. The stated objective is to establish a dynamic, real-time and future-ready official statistical architecture. The announcement referred to greater timeliness, data granularity, interoperability and the development of harmonised, AI-ready datasets.

These terms describe different aspects of data infrastructure. Timeliness concerns how quickly information becomes available after the event or period it measures. Granularity concerns the level of detail, such as whether a statistic can be examined at a more local or sector-specific level. Interoperability means that systems can exchange and use information through compatible standards. Harmonisation seeks to make definitions and classifications sufficiently consistent for meaningful comparison. AI-ready does not mean that an algorithm can be trusted without oversight; it suggests that datasets are organised for analytical use, while questions of quality, privacy and accountability remain.

The release also described strategic flexibility to allocate resources according to immediate policy needs and a broad programme involving surveys, methodological research, digital transformation and national data governance. Each activity has a different success test. A survey should use a defensible sample and publish its methodology. A digital platform should protect data and record changes. A common classification should improve comparability without erasing legitimate differences between populations or sectors.

An allocation is an input, not an outcome. The VISTAR approval creates a policy framework and financial commitment over five financial years. It does not by itself establish that every dataset will become real-time, that all agencies will adopt common systems or that analytical decisions will improve. Those claims require implementation evidence. The central test will be whether more reliable and accessible official statistics help institutions make better decisions while preserving the independence, confidentiality and methodological integrity on which public trust depends.

passages.title: Building domestic processing capacity for critical minerals

sources.title: Cabinet Approves Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing with an Outlay of Rs.2,814 Crore for Lithium and Nickel processing
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India

passages.text:
Critical minerals support a wide range of modern industries. Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries, while nickel is important in battery materials, alloys and other industrial applications. A country may possess mineral resources yet remain dependent on overseas suppliers for refined intermediates or high-purity processed materials. Mining and processing are distinct stages: extracting an ore does not automatically create the chemical or metallurgical product required by a battery or industrial manufacturer.

On 4 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved the Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing, with a financial outlay of ₹2,814 crore over five years, from FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31. The Press Information Bureau stated that the scheme would support four processing plants: two lithium plants with a minimum capacity of 30 kilotonnes each and two nickel plants with a minimum capacity of 50 kilotonnes each. It provides a capital subsidy of 30 per cent of eligible investment, subject to specified caps and conditions. The release described support ceilings of ₹500 crore per lithium beneficiary and ₹900 crore per nickel beneficiary.

Selection is designed as a two-stage process. Applicants are first assessed for technical qualification. Only those that qualify technically proceed to financial bidding. For each mineral, two beneficiaries are to be selected using a least-cost criterion, based on the lowest capital support sought by bidders. The subsidy is to be disbursed in three tranches linked to specified milestones. These features are intended to combine a minimum technical threshold with competition over the amount of public support requested.

The economic rationale concerns supply-chain resilience. Concentrated processing capacity can expose downstream industries to geopolitical disruption, price volatility or export restrictions. Domestic facilities may reduce one form of vulnerability, but they do not make a country self-sufficient in every input. Processing plants still require suitable feedstock, energy, water, skilled workers, technology, environmental safeguards and buyers for their output. The financial viability of a plant depends on more than the announced subsidy.

The scheme should therefore be assessed through actual investment, capacity commissioned, product quality, environmental performance and the extent to which domestic users obtain dependable supplies. The announcement signals an industrial policy preference for building a missing link in the value chain. Whether that preference becomes durable capability will depend on project execution, competitive selection and the development of a wider ecosystem around the plants.

passages.title: Grid-scale storage and the renewable electricity system

sources.title: Cabinet approves Rs.14,500 crore Viability Gap Funding Scheme for development of 92 GWh Grid-Scale Energy Storage Systems
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India

passages.text:
Electricity systems must balance supply and demand continuously. Solar and wind generation can vary with weather and time of day, while consumers expect power to be available when they need it. Energy storage can help by absorbing electricity when supply is abundant and releasing it later. Storage does not create energy; it shifts availability across time and can provide services that support grid stability. Different technologies have different operating characteristics, costs, environmental effects and suitable locations.

On 4 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved a Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme for development of grid-scale energy storage systems. The Press Information Bureau reported total financial support of ₹14,500 crore for FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31. The scheme aims to support 92 gigawatt-hours of energy-storage capacity that is yet to be commissioned. The announced composition comprises 30 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), 60 GWh of Pumped Storage Projects and 2 GWh of emerging storage technologies. The release also stated that the scheme would include a domestic-content requirement for BESS.

VGF is a form of public support intended to make an otherwise difficult project financially viable, particularly where social or system benefits may not be fully reflected in the revenue available to a private investor. It is not the same as paying the entire cost of a project. A project still needs financing, construction, land or site access, grid connection, technical approvals and competent operation. The amount of storage measured in GWh describes energy capacity; the ability to deliver power at a particular rate is a separate characteristic, often expressed in gigawatts.

The mix of technologies matters. Batteries can respond quickly and may be deployed in modular installations. Pumped storage uses electricity to move water to a higher reservoir and later releases it through turbines, but suitable geography and environmental assessment are essential. Emerging technologies may diversify options, although commercial readiness and operating performance vary. Domestic-content conditions can encourage manufacturing and local supply chains, while procurement rules must still preserve quality and cost discipline.

The government described the programme as a way to integrate renewable energy, strengthen grid stability and support reliable, affordable round-the-clock electricity. These are intended benefits rather than results already achieved. Evaluation should examine commissioned capacity, actual utilisation, system costs, environmental impacts and whether storage reduces curtailment or improves reliability. The value of the scheme will be measured by dependable services delivered to the grid, not simply by the capacity announced at approval.

passages.title: RBI review of priority sector lending instructions

sources.title: Consolidation of Instructions Related to Priority Sector Lending – Drafts for Comments

passages.text:
Priority Sector Lending (PSL) is a regulatory framework through which banks are directed to allocate a specified share of credit to sectors and activities identified as important for broad-based development and financial inclusion. The framework recognises that commercial lending decisions may not, on their own, provide adequate access to credit for some groups or activities. Classification rules and targets are therefore used to shape how regulated institutions report and fulfil their lending obligations.

On 5 November 2026, the Reserve Bank of India announced that it had reviewed existing PSL instructions and placed consolidated draft Directions on its website for public comments. The drafts are organised separately for commercial banks, small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks and urban co-operative banks. The RBI stated that instructions not included in the consolidated drafts would be repealed consequent to issuance of the Directions, with the repeal to be notified separately. Comments were invited on or before 26 November 2026 through the Connect 2 Regulate section or the specified email channel.

The announcement is a draft-stage regulatory exercise. It should not be read as though every proposed provision had already become binding. A consultation allows regulated entities, borrowers, industry bodies and other interested parties to identify implementation difficulties, suggest clearer wording and point out unintended consequences. The regulator can consider the feedback before finalising the Directions. The exact legal effect begins only in accordance with the final instrument and its commencement provisions.

Consolidation can improve usability when an institution must consult instructions issued at different times. A single, organised set of Directions may reduce the risk that a bank overlooks a relevant circular or applies an outdated classification. But combining instructions is not merely a formatting exercise. Definitions, exclusions, reporting requirements and transition dates must be handled carefully, especially where different categories of regulated entities operate under different business models.

The wider policy objective is to make lending rules clearer while preserving the intended access to priority sectors. A sound assessment would examine whether the final rules improve compliance, data quality and credit availability without creating arbitrary incentives or weakening prudential standards. The 5 November announcement marks the beginning of consultation on draft texts; it does not itself establish the final rules or demonstrate any change in the volume of credit reaching borrowers.

passages.title: Household inflation expectations as an input to monetary policy

sources.title: RBI launches the November 2026 round of the Inflation Expectations Survey of Households

passages.text:
Inflation statistics generally describe changes in the prices of a basket of goods and services. Households, however, experience prices through their own spending patterns. A family that spends a large share of its budget on food may notice a different pattern from a household whose major expenses are rent, transport or education. Expectations about future prices can influence decisions such as whether to save, borrow, postpone a purchase or ask for a higher wage.

On 3 November 2026, the Reserve Bank of India announced the launch of the November round of its Inflation Expectations Survey of Households. The survey covers 19 cities, including Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Kolkata and several other urban centres. It seeks qualitative responses about perceived price changes in general and in specific product groups over the next three months and one year. It also seeks quantitative responses about current inflation and expected inflation over those same horizons. The RBI stated that the results provide useful inputs for monetary policy.

A household survey measures expectations, not the official inflation rate itself. Respondents may have limited information, may focus on recent price changes or may interpret a question differently. Their answers can still be informative because expectations are part of the environment in which households and businesses make decisions. A policymaker may compare survey responses with observed prices, wage developments, market indicators and other surveys rather than treat any single response as a forecast that must come true.

The difference between qualitative and quantitative questions is important. A qualitative answer may indicate that prices are expected to rise faster, rise more slowly or remain broadly unchanged. A quantitative answer asks respondents to attach a numerical rate to their expectation. Neither approach is automatically superior: qualitative responses can capture direction and breadth, while numerical responses provide a stated magnitude but may be harder for some respondents to estimate accurately.

A survey’s usefulness depends on its sampling design, question wording, geographic coverage, response quality and consistency across rounds. The 19-city coverage should not be mistaken for a census of every Indian household. Nor does the launch announcement provide the survey’s final results. The exercise offers one source of evidence about how households perceive prices; monetary policy must weigh that evidence alongside measured inflation, economic activity and the broader outlook.

passages.title: The rule of disclosed reasons in public decisions
passages.text:
A public authority may grant a licence, impose a penalty or refuse an application only after considering the material that the governing rule permits it to consider. For this exercise, assume the following principle: where a decision materially affects an individual’s rights or legitimate interests, the authority must give written reasons that identify the decisive facts and explain how the applicable rule was applied. The reasons need not answer every sentence submitted by the applicant, but they must be sufficiently specific to permit an effective appeal. A decision based on a factor that the rule expressly excludes is invalid.

The principle does not require a hearing in every routine administrative act. A separate rule may provide that an emergency measure can be imposed immediately where delay would create a serious and imminent risk, provided the authority records the risk and offers a prompt post-decision opportunity to respond. The emergency exception is narrow: administrative convenience, staff shortage or a desire to finish a file quickly does not qualify as an imminent risk.

Suppose a transport authority suspends a ferry operator’s permit after a documented inspection finds repeated failures of emergency equipment. The authority states the inspection dates, identifies the failed equipment and explains that the permit condition requires functional safety systems. Those reasons may satisfy the principle even if the operator disputes the inspector’s conclusion, because the decision identifies the evidence and the rule applied. The dispute can then be examined on appeal.

Now suppose the authority refuses a permit renewal because an applicant criticised the department in a newspaper, although the governing rule lists only safety, financial capacity and technical competence as relevant factors. The authority’s reasons may be detailed, but the decision still relies on an excluded consideration. Giving reasons does not cure the use of an unlawful factor. Conversely, a decision may use a relevant factor but remain defective if the authority gives only a formulaic statement such as ‘not in the public interest’ without explaining the facts.

The principle seeks accountable administration rather than perfect writing. An appellate body should ask whether the affected person can understand why the decision was made and challenge the decisive basis. It should not substitute its own preferred policy merely because another conclusion was possible. The focus is the connection between the permitted rule, the material facts and the reasons communicated.

passages.title: Contract variation and informed consent
passages.text:
Assume a contractual principle with the following terms. A valid variation requires agreement by both parties to the new obligation, communicated before the changed performance is due. Agreement may be express or inferred from conduct, but silence alone is not acceptance unless the parties previously agreed that silence would have that effect. A party that performs the new obligation after receiving clear notice of the proposed change may be treated as having accepted it, provided the conduct is not equally consistent with the original contract.

The principle also distinguishes a request from a variation. One party may ask for a different delivery date, price or specification. The request does not change the contract until the other party accepts it. A party cannot unilaterally impose a new term merely by sending an email stating that the contract has been amended. Nor can an agreement be inferred where the receiving party immediately objects and continues to perform only the original obligation.

Consider a supplier required to deliver 500 standard chairs by 1 June. On 10 May, the purchaser proposes that the supplier deliver 300 ergonomic chairs instead, at an agreed additional price. The supplier replies, ‘We accept the revised quantity, specification and price,’ and both parties adjust their production plans. The variation is effective because the new obligations were clearly accepted before performance became due.

In a different case, the purchaser sends a message saying that the delivery date has been moved forward by two weeks. The supplier does not reply but delivers on the original date. Silence does not establish acceptance, and the conduct is consistent with the original contract. The purchaser cannot claim that the earlier date became binding merely because it sent a message.

A more difficult case arises where the supplier, after receiving a clear proposal, begins manufacturing the revised product without replying. The conduct may support an inference of acceptance if it is objectively consistent with the proposed variation and inconsistent with the original order. But the conclusion depends on context: if the supplier was already scheduled to manufacture similar products under the original contract, the same conduct may not prove agreement. The decision-maker must examine communication, timing and the practical meaning of performance rather than presume that every action signifies consent.

The parties' records should therefore be read as a sequence: proposal, communication, response and performance. No single document controls in isolation where the surrounding conduct makes the parties' shared understanding clear.

passages.title: Reasonable accommodation in access to a service
passages.text:
For this problem, assume the following access principle. A service provider open to the public must make reasonable adjustments for a person with a disability where an adjustment is practical, does not remove an essential requirement of the service and does not impose a disproportionate burden. The provider must consider the individual request and relevant evidence; it cannot reject all adjustments by relying on a blanket policy. The person requesting an adjustment should explain the barrier and cooperate with reasonable requests for information.

An adjustment may change the method by which a service is delivered without changing the substantive standard. A college, for example, may allow a student with a mobility impairment to use an accessible entrance or may provide a digital copy of a reading list. It need not waive an examination’s essential learning outcomes merely because a student requests a different assessment. The distinction is between removing an avoidable barrier and removing the core purpose of the service.

The burden assessment must be concrete. A provider should consider cost, available resources, frequency of the request, safety and the effect on other users. A modest adjustment that can be implemented through an existing system is unlikely to be disproportionate merely because it requires staff to change a routine. An adjustment that would require rebuilding an entire facility within a few days may be disproportionate in the circumstances, though the provider should still explore an interim alternative.

Suppose a public museum has a step-free side entrance that staff can unlock on request. A visitor using a wheelchair asks to use it. A policy requiring all visitors to use the front stairs would be difficult to justify because the requested adjustment is practical and preserves the museum’s ordinary access rules. If the side entrance is temporarily blocked by an emergency repair, staff should consider another safe route or a reasonable alternative rather than simply refusing entry.

The principle does not guarantee the exact adjustment preferred by the requester. It requires a genuine assessment and a response that addresses the barrier without defeating an essential requirement. A provider that explains why one proposal is impractical and offers an effective alternative may comply. A provider that refuses to engage, or relies only on the inconvenience of changing its routine, does not.

The provider should record the reasons for its assessment so that the requester can understand which barrier was considered and why the chosen response is effective. A reasoned process also helps the provider apply the same standard consistently to later requests.

passages.title: Privacy, purpose limitation and retained records
passages.text:
Assume a data-handling principle for this passage. An organisation that collects personal information for a stated purpose may use it only for that purpose or for a closely related purpose that a reasonable person would expect. It must collect no more information than is reasonably necessary and must delete or anonymise identifiable records when they are no longer needed, unless a separate legal retention duty applies. A person must be told, in clear terms, what information is collected and why.

The principle recognises that some records have more than one legitimate use. A clinic may collect a patient’s contact details to arrange appointments and may use those details to send a reminder about a scheduled visit. It cannot automatically use the same details to promote an unrelated commercial product. A school may keep attendance records for administration, but publishing an identifiable list of students with repeated absences would require a separate justification and may cause harm.

Necessity is assessed in relation to the purpose. A library that needs to notify a borrower about an overdue book may require a contact method and a record of the loan. It may not need to collect the borrower’s precise location throughout the day. A service provider may retain a limited transaction record for a defined period to resolve disputes or comply with a legal duty, but retaining every detail indefinitely because storage is cheap does not satisfy the principle.

Suppose a fitness application collects a user’s step count to display activity trends. It then shares identifiable daily location histories with an advertising company, although users were told only that the data would support activity tracking. The sharing is not closely related to the stated purpose and is not reasonably expected. A broad statement that the application may ‘improve services’ would not necessarily make the secondary use clear.

The principle requires a practical connection among notice, collection, use and retention. It does not prohibit all secondary uses, nor does it require deletion where another law demands preservation. The decision-maker should identify the purpose communicated to the person, the information actually collected, the proposed use and any specific retention obligation. A general claim that data might be useful in the future is not enough to justify unlimited collection or indefinite retention.

An organisation should be able to explain why each category of information is needed and how long it will be kept. A retention schedule linked to the original purpose is more defensible than an open-ended policy based on possible future usefulness.

passages.title: Consumer claims and fair opportunity to respond
passages.text:
Assume a consumer-protection principle for this exercise. A trader who makes a specific factual claim about a product must possess a reasonable basis for the claim at the time it is made. If a customer complains that the product materially fails to match the claim, the trader must investigate relevant evidence and provide a fair opportunity to resolve the dispute. A trader need not accept every complaint, but cannot dismiss it solely because the customer did not use the trader’s preferred wording or channel where the complaint was otherwise clearly received.

A claim is factual when it can be tested against evidence, such as a stated capacity, material, performance level or warranty period. General expressions of praise may be opinion, but an objectively measurable statement cannot be converted into opinion simply by placing it in an advertisement. The reasonable-basis requirement is assessed at the time the claim is published. A later successful test does not necessarily prove that the trader had a proper basis earlier.

The response obligation is procedural as well as substantive. The trader should identify the complaint, consider the product information and relevant records, and communicate a reasoned outcome. A customer may be asked to provide a receipt or serial number where that information is reasonably needed. The trader should not demand irrelevant personal data or impose a procedure that makes a genuine complaint practically impossible to submit.

Suppose an advertisement states that a water filter removes 99 per cent of a named contaminant under specified test conditions. The trader relies on a laboratory report using the same model and conditions. A customer later reports that a unit appears defective. The report may provide a reasonable basis for the general advertisement, but it does not conclusively establish that the customer’s particular unit works correctly. The trader must examine the individual complaint.

If another trader advertises the same result without testing, supplier evidence or a credible technical basis, the claim may be unsupported even if it later happens to be accurate. Conversely, a single unusual complaint does not prove that every product is defective. The principle asks whether the factual claim was responsibly supported and whether the later complaint was considered fairly, not whether every dispute must end in a refund.

A fair process also requires the trader to distinguish a defect allegation from a question about the general design of the product. Evidence relevant to one may not resolve the other, and the response should identify which issue has actually been examined.

passages.title: Shared property and temporary emergency access
passages.text:
Assume the following property principle. A person who has a lawful right to use shared property must not unreasonably prevent another authorised user from exercising an equivalent right. Temporary restrictions may be justified where they are necessary to prevent an immediate risk to people or property, but the restriction must be proportionate in scope and duration. The person imposing it should communicate the reason and restore ordinary access when the risk ends.

Shared property may include a common corridor, driveway, stairwell, loading bay or facility maintained for several users. An authorised user does not acquire exclusive control merely because that person uses the space frequently. At the same time, equal access does not mean that every person may use the property in any manner. Posted safety rules and reasonable scheduling arrangements may regulate access if they apply fairly and preserve the essential shared use.

Consider an apartment building where residents have a shared driveway. One resident leaves a vehicle across the only emergency exit for several hours. The building manager may arrange immediate removal because the obstruction creates a serious risk and prevents others from using the driveway safely. The action should be limited to what is needed to clear the obstruction; it does not create a permanent right for the manager to reserve the driveway for one resident.

In another situation, a resident places a small package in a marked loading area for five minutes while carrying groceries upstairs. If the rules permit brief loading and no emergency access is blocked, another resident cannot claim a general right to remove the package merely because that resident prefers the area to remain empty. The relevant question is whether the use is authorised and whether it materially interferes with another user’s equivalent right.

The emergency exception should not become a convenient tool for exclusion. A person invoking it must point to a real and immediate risk, not a speculative possibility or personal disagreement. Once the risk is controlled, normal access should return. A decision-maker should therefore examine the nature of the shared right, the actual interference, the urgency of the risk and the duration of the restriction.

The principle does not prevent reasonable time slots or safety arrangements where they apply evenly and leave a meaningful opportunity for each authorised user. It prevents one user from converting shared access into private control without a justification grounded in the stated rule.

passages.title: The argument for later library opening hours
passages.text:
A municipal committee is considering whether to keep three public libraries open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. The proposal is supported by a survey in which 62 per cent of respondents who work full-time said that current opening hours make it difficult to visit. The committee chair argues that extending hours will increase access because people who cannot arrive before 6 p.m. will gain an additional opportunity to use the libraries. The proposal would require evening staffing and higher security costs.

Opponents argue that the survey does not establish the likely number of additional visitors. Some respondents may prefer weekend hours, while others may not visit even if the libraries remain open later. They also note that electricity, transport and staffing costs could reduce the amount available for new books and maintenance. The chair replies that access should be assessed by whether an opportunity exists, not only by whether every available hour is fully used.

A third committee member proposes a six-month pilot in one library, with opening hours extended to 10 p.m. on three weekdays. The pilot would record visits by time of day, lending activity, programme attendance and user feedback. It would also compare the additional staffing and security costs with the costs of other ways to improve access, such as a mobile library or longer weekend opening. The member argues that the pilot would provide better evidence than either side currently possesses.

The proposal raises several distinct questions. The survey supports the claim that current hours create a barrier for some full-time workers, but it does not quantify how many would use a later service. A pilot could test demand, although one branch may not represent every neighbourhood. A full cost comparison would need to consider not only expenditure but also who benefits and whether alternative services reach the same users.

The chair warns that an experiment should not become an excuse to postpone a decision indefinitely. The pilot should therefore have a fixed duration, publicly stated evaluation criteria and a date on which the committee must decide whether to expand, modify or end the arrangement. The argument for later hours is strongest when it acknowledges uncertainty and sets out a way to learn from actual use rather than relying solely on stated preferences.

A useful evaluation would also distinguish first-time evening visitors from people who shift their existing visits to a later hour. Without that distinction, the committee could mistake a change in timing for an overall increase in access.

passages.title: Do electric buses always reduce urban emissions?
passages.text:
A transport authority proposes replacing diesel buses with electric buses on a group of city routes. Its report states that electric buses have no tailpipe emissions and can reduce local exposure to exhaust pollutants. The authority concludes that the programme will reduce the environmental impact of public transport. A councillor supports the proposal but warns that the conclusion depends on how the electricity is generated, how batteries are produced and what happens to them at the end of their service life.

The authority responds that the buses will operate for many years and that the electricity grid is gradually adding renewable generation. It argues that a comparison should consider the entire operating life rather than treat the current electricity mix as fixed. A second councillor asks whether the new buses will replace existing diesel services or merely add capacity to routes that are already well served. If the new fleet is additional, the total number of vehicle journeys could rise even if each electric bus is cleaner in operation.

A transport researcher suggests that the authority publish a route-level evaluation. It should record energy use, passenger numbers, vehicle-kilometres, electricity sources and maintenance needs. The study should compare the electric fleet with the diesel buses that would otherwise have operated, while also considering whether service improvements attract passengers away from private vehicles. The researcher argues that an electric bus can deliver a larger climate benefit when it replaces car journeys than when it simply replaces a nearly empty bus.

The discussion illustrates why a technology label is not a complete environmental assessment. Tailpipe emissions are only one part of the impact. Electricity generation and manufacturing matter, but so do occupancy, route design and the alternative mode of travel. A city should not ignore immediate air-quality benefits merely because life-cycle analysis is complex. Nor should it claim a precise reduction without stating the comparison and assumptions.

The authority decides to publish both operational emissions and a life-cycle estimate, and to report passenger changes separately. This approach will not answer every value question, such as how much the city should spend to improve air quality, but it will make the evidence underlying the decision more transparent.

The comparison should also state whether battery replacement and end-of-life treatment are included, since excluding those stages could make one option appear cleaner simply because part of its impact occurs outside the route's operating budget.

passages.title: The limits of a school ranking
passages.text:
A newspaper publishes a ranking of secondary schools based on examination results. The highest-ranked schools have the largest share of students achieving top grades. A commentator argues that parents should use the ranking to identify the strongest schools because examination results are a direct measure of academic performance. A head teacher agrees that results matter but says the ranking does not account for the starting points of students, the resources available to schools or the breadth of the curriculum.

The newspaper replies that a ranking must use a common measure if readers are to compare institutions. It adds that parents can consult other information before making a decision. A parent association asks whether the results are adjusted for student intake and whether the ranking includes students who transferred out before the examinations. It also asks whether schools with small cohorts are ranked in the same way as schools with several hundred candidates.

An education analyst proposes publishing several indicators rather than one league table. These would include examination progress from an earlier baseline, attendance, student wellbeing, access to arts and sport, teacher retention and the proportion of students completing different subjects. The analyst does not suggest that every indicator can be combined into a single score. Instead, the information would allow parents to ask which features matter most for a particular child.

The head teacher accepts that examination results should remain visible, but argues that a school should not be judged only by the proportion of top grades. A school serving students who begin with significant learning gaps may produce substantial progress without matching the final results of a selective institution. The newspaper responds that measuring progress requires reliable baseline data and may be harder for families to interpret than final grades.

The dispute is not between measurement and no measurement. It concerns whether a single measure can fairly stand for a broad educational purpose. A transparent ranking can reveal useful information, but users should know what it includes, what it omits and how the underlying data were collected. The more consequential the decision, the less safe it is to confuse a convenient comparison with a complete evaluation.

The analyst's approach also requires safeguards against misleading comparisons: baseline measures must be collected consistently, missing students must be accounted for, and small cohorts should be accompanied by uncertainty information rather than ranked as though every percentage were equally stable.

passages.title: A pilot programme for rooftop gardens
passages.text:
A housing cooperative is considering a rooftop garden on one of its apartment buildings. Supporters say the garden could reduce roof temperatures, provide residents with a shared activity and improve storm-water absorption. They cite a small demonstration at another building where participants reported that the roof felt cooler and that they used the space several times a week. Opponents question whether the proposed roof can safely carry the additional load and whether residents will maintain the garden after the initial enthusiasm fades.

The cooperative’s engineer says that the roof must be assessed for structural capacity, waterproofing and drainage before any installation. The engineer also notes that a lightweight container system would impose a different load from deep soil beds. The garden committee argues that the project could begin with a limited pilot using lightweight containers and a small group of volunteer residents. It proposes collecting temperature readings, maintenance hours and records of water use for one summer.

A resident who supports the project warns that a pilot might understate the benefits because a small garden will provide less shade than a full installation. A sceptical resident replies that a large project would create greater financial and safety risks if the assumptions prove wrong. Both agree that the cooperative should first establish who will be responsible for watering, repairs and access, and how the costs will be divided among residents.

The cooperative’s manager points out that the demonstration building differs in roof design and climate exposure. The reported sense of coolness is useful feedback but is not a substitute for measured temperature data. The pilot should include a comparison area on the same roof, where feasible, and should record weather conditions so that changes are not attributed to the garden when they result from a cooler week.

The proposal is therefore conditional. A structural assessment and a clear maintenance plan are necessary before the pilot begins. If those requirements are met, a limited trial can test practical questions without assuming that the experience of another building will automatically transfer. The decision should depend on safety, measurable outcomes, costs and the willingness of residents to maintain the space.

The cooperative should also decide how residents who cannot participate in gardening can still use the roof and how access will be managed during maintenance. These operational questions affect whether the project remains a shared amenity rather than becoming the preserve of a small volunteer group.

passages.title: Community water use
passages.text:

| A | 120 | 132 | 126 | 138 | 144 |
| B | 90 | 96 | 102 | 99 | 108 |

The ward's weekly distribution target is 2,600 thousand litres across all four zones. Treat each listed figure as the actual volume distributed on that day. For percentage calculations, use the exact values rather than rounded averages.

passages.title: A public transport pass scheme
passages.text:
A city offers monthly travel passes under three categories. A Standard pass costs ₹900 and permits 40 trips; a Concession pass costs ₹540 and permits 30 trips; a Flex pass costs ₹1,200 and permits unlimited trips. During one month, the authority sells 2,400 Standard passes, 1,500 Concession passes and 900 Flex passes.

Assume all passes are sold at the listed price. For a revenue estimate, count only pass sales and ignore transaction fees. In a separate pilot, 600 Standard pass holders each make 32 trips, 300 Concession pass holders each make 24 trips, and 200 Flex pass holders each make an average of 46 trips. Treat the pilot sample as separate from the monthly sales totals.

passages.title: Solar installation at public buildings
passages.text:
A district installs rooftop solar systems at 12 public buildings. Each building has a system rated at 25 kW. On a representative sunny day, each kW generates 4.2 kWh of electricity. The combined installation cost is ₹1.08 crore. The district pays ₹6 per kWh for electricity purchased from the grid.

Assume the systems generate at the stated rate on 300 days per year and produce no credited surplus on the remaining days. Ignore maintenance, financing costs and degradation for this exercise. Treat each kWh generated as replacing one kWh that would otherwise have been purchased from the grid.
